prize_parts.citation: For establishing that liquid-liquid phase separation of multivalent biomolecules is a physical-chemical principle by which cells organise their interior without membranes.

statement.case_for: After round 1 my scientific case is unchanged, but I have narrowed what it asks the committee to honour. The founding results are two: P granules behave as liquids that dissolve and condense with concentration (Brangwynne and Hyman), and defined multivalent proteins and RNA undergo a sharp, tunable phase transition in vitro whose boundary follows valency and affinity (Rosen). Both are standard thermodynamics applied to biomolecules, and both were tested quantitatively by groups other than their authors. The concept has changed how chemists and biologists think about intracellular organisation, and it now frames work on neurodegeneration and on drug partitioning into condensates. The prize would credit a principle of molecular organisation, not every later use of the word condensate. That is the kind of discovery in which physical chemistry has been under-recognised relative to synthesis and structure.
statement.case_against: The critique repeated in round 1 is fair for most in vivo claims: overexpression, imaging-only evidence and loose use of the label, plus a dense-phase structure that is poorly defined at the molecular level. A prize freezes a framing that is still moving, and Chabes, Zou and Linke want quantitative evidence of function in cells. The three-person limit also leaves out Pappu and Mittag, who supplied the sequence grammar and the physical theory, and I cannot show that this omission is clean. Finally, B052 has only my own support, no majority path in round 1, and it may be seen as closer to biology than to chemistry. Whether to prefer a candidate that is more settled now is a legitimate judgement, and B060 is the one I would turn to.

responses.point: Andrei says many in vivo condensates rest on overexpression and imaging with few quantitative tests of function, and that a prize would freeze an interpretation still moving.
responses.response: In round 1 I asked for a specific control that the founding work fails, and he did not name one; his objection is to the later literature. I now concede something to him: the citation should not mention cells as a whole or function, only the liquid-like organisation and the in vitro phase behaviour, so that it does not freeze the contested in vivo claims. Where we still differ is that I treat a field-wide quality problem as a reason for careful wording, not for waiting, because the thermodynamic criteria (a concentration threshold, a tie line, a measurable interfacial tension) are exactly what can separate the sound cases from the weak ones.

responses.point: Xiaodong asks for structural rigour: the dense phase is poorly defined at the molecular level, and she contrasts it with certified and structurally characterised perovskites.
responses.response: This is a fair criterion for a materials discovery, but a liquid phase has no lattice, so atomic structure cannot be the test; the test is thermodynamic and kinetic. For Rosen's defined systems and for P-granule fusion and wetting, those quantities have been measured, and NMR and scattering show a dense phase that is dynamic and heterogeneous, which is what a condensed liquid should be. I accept that the molecular grammar inside dense phases is less complete than the crystal chemistry of perovskites, and that is why I also see B010 as a more settled case on structure. I do not think it makes B052 less chemical.

responses.point: Heiner finds the physics compelling but wants quantitative evidence of function in cells before it enters a citation, and sees the omission of Pappu and Mittag as a problem; his own first choice is B039.
responses.response: I have adopted his request on the citation: my wording now speaks of a physical-chemical principle of organisation and says nothing about cellular function. On credit, I agree the cut is imperfect. Nanopores have the same problem, since a three-person cut omits Branton or Kasianowicz, so imperfect attribution cannot be what separates our candidates. I would ask him instead whether he sees B039 as chemistry and not analytical physics, because that was the open question in the chair's summary and it is the same kind of boundary question he raises about B052.

responses.point: Peter says a prize should honour a settled discovery and that he cannot name a chemical transformation or method in condensates the way he can for coupling or base editing.
responses.response: He is right that there is no transformation or reagent here, and that is the substance of my disagreement with his framing, not a flaw in it: the 1980s to 2010s chemistry prizes have rewarded concepts of molecular organisation as well as methods, and the committee should be willing to do so. On settledness, the founding reconstitution and P-granule experiments are settled; the extent of in vivo use is not. I do see his point that B023 has the clearest record, and I would not object to it as a prize, although its novelty relative to 2010 is small.

responses.point: Johan lists B052 eighth and says Rosen, Pappu and Mittag are all essential, and that the placement between chemistry and biology is uncertain, and he says credit among B066 lipid contributors is tangled.
responses.response: I accept his point on B066: in my own field I can see Cullis's group and the later Anderson and Langer work as distinct steps, and I cannot defend a clean three either, so I have kept B066 out of my configuration. I take his point about Rosen, Pappu and Mittag as the best argument against my three names, but a prize cannot reach all of them, and Rosen's quantitative in vitro work is the closest to a direct physical measurement. If the committee prefers theory to be credited, I would be open to discussing whether Pappu replaces Rosen, though I would still want Brangwynne and Hyman.

responses.point: Peter pairs B030 with B060, says condensates are unsettled on mechanism and function, and notes that I flagged the debate myself.
responses.response: I did flag the debate, and I do not hide it. I disagree that unsettled in vivo mechanism means the in vitro mechanism is unsettled, because that part is a measured phase diagram. His own B030 is a mature field with an excellent record, but it is a priority-clean achievement whose conceptual outline was set by Marcus theory, and I cannot see it gathering a majority from the opening ballots. On B060, he and others have made the strongest case for an alternative to mine, and that is the configuration I would move to if B052 cannot get a majority.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that the founding in vitro and P-granule results stand independently of the unresolved in vivo debate
Whether omitting Pappu and Mittag is acceptable, and whether Rosen or Pappu is the better third name
Whether B052 is Chemistry or Physiology or Medicine, which I cannot settle from the dossiers
Whether B060 can become a stable five-vote configuration, since its supporters pair it with three different partners and whether Komor and Gaudelli should be named beside Liu is open
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. No personal, institutional, mentor or collaborator tie to any credited name on the shortlist is stated in my profile. My field is close to B052 and B066, which I note for transparency, I share a Lund tradition with Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai, and my protein self-assembly interests overlap with those of Daniel Aili, though none of these is a tie to a candidate.
